items.originalTitle: Godot will no longer accept AI-authored code contributions
items.summary:
The Godot Foundation has announced a new policy banning AI-authored code contributions and AI-generated text in communications to alleviate the burden on maintainers and ensure accountability. This decision comes after maintainers faced increasing challenges reviewing AI-generated pull requests, which they found draining and demoralizing. The Foundation emphasized that contributions must come from humans who understand and take responsibility for their code, as AI cannot be held accountable for fixing issues.

The policy update aims to reduce low-effort contributions and foster a sustainable environment where maintainers can mentor new contributors effectively. While AI assistance for minor tasks is allowed with disclosure, the Foundation will reject AI-generated code and text in human interactions to maintain respect and quality in the project. The Foundation plans to continue monitoring AI developments and adjust policies as needed.

items.title: Claude launches Claude Science, an AI-powered research platform for reproducible scientific analysis and manuscript drafting, available on macOS and Linux [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Science
items.summary:
Claude has launched Claude Science, an AI-powered research platform designed to support rigorous scientific analysis and manuscript drafting. Available on macOS and Linux, the platform enables researchers to run analyses, search databases, and trace every step from data processing to publication, ensuring full reproducibility and transparency. It integrates native scientific renderers and automated fact-checking to enhance accuracy and efficiency in research workflows.

The platform is pre-configured for various life science domains, including genomics, proteomics, and cheminformatics, and supports complex tasks such as single-cell RNA-seq analysis, phylogenetic studies, and protein structure exploration. Claude Science manages computing resources across local machines and HPC clusters, allowing seamless scaling and persistent computational sessions. Users can draft manuscripts alongside their analyses, with all figures and data linked to the underlying code and environment for easy iteration and verification.

By combining AI capabilities with domain-specific tools and databases, Claude Science aims to transform scientific research by making complex analyses more accessible and reproducible. Early users have highlighted its ability to uncover insights and streamline workflows, suggesting it could become a valuable asset for multidisciplinary research teams.

items.title: Meta AI releases Brain2Qwerty v2, a non-invasive AI system decoding real-time sentences from brain waves with up to 78% word accuracy, approaching surgical method performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From brain waves to words: a new path to communication without surgery
items.summary:
Meta AI has introduced Brain2Qwerty v2, an advanced non-invasive AI system that decodes real-time sentences from brain waves with up to 78% word accuracy, nearing the performance of invasive surgical methods. This technology uses magnetoencephalography (MEG) to record brain activity and employs end-to-end deep learning combined with large language models to translate neural signals into coherent text.

Trained on extensive data from volunteer participants, Brain2Qwerty v2 significantly outperforms previous non-invasive approaches, which had much lower accuracy rates. The system's accuracy improves with more data, suggesting that further advancements could close the gap with surgical techniques. Meta AI has released the training code and datasets to encourage open research and accelerate progress in neuroscience, aiming to aid individuals with communication impairments caused by brain lesions.

items.title: GLM-5.2's code review accuracy varies significantly based on prompt wording, with better results on simpler codebases and more inconsistency on complex projects [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GLM-5.2's Code Reviews Are Only as Good as Your Prompt
items.summary:
GLM-5.2, an open-weight AI model from Z.ai, shows varying accuracy in code reviews depending on the prompt wording and complexity of the codebase. In tests using a TypeScript backend with planted bugs, the model consistently identified most security issues in simpler projects regardless of prompt style or reasoning effort. However, its performance became less reliable on a more complex codebase with subtler bugs that required deeper understanding of product rules and feature behavior.

The evaluation involved three different prompt framings—casual, consistency-focused, and strict production—and multiple reasoning effort levels. While GLM-5.2 caught nearly all serious bugs in the straightforward codebase, its ability to detect nuanced errors like incorrect optimistic locking or permission guards diminished on the expanded project. This suggests that prompt design and code complexity significantly influence the model's effectiveness in automated code auditing.

items.summary:
Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5, a language model ranked fifth in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, demonstrates improved performance over some higher-priced models but consumes about 40% more tokens per task than its predecessor. Despite maintaining the same token pricing, this increased token usage effectively raises the real cost per task, continuing a pattern of hidden price increases by Anthropic.

The model's higher token consumption is partly due to its more agentic behavior, which leads to more agent loops in tasks, and a tokenizer change that inflates token counts. While Sonnet 5 shows gains in several benchmarks, it still lags behind larger models in complex reasoning tests. This pricing strategy contrasts with competitors offering competitive performance at lower costs, highlighting the need for more transparent pricing based on standardized tasks rather than raw token rates.

items.originalTitle: Why your AI bill is bigger than it should be
items.summary:
LeadDev reports that inflated AI bills often result from inefficient data processing and excessive token usage when interacting with large language models (LLMs). An engineer's experience with a costly debugging session led to the creation of Headroom, an open-source tool that optimizes context compression and reduces unnecessary data sent to AI models. This innovation has saved users approximately $700,000 in five months by improving token efficiency and providing better visibility into AI spending.

Headroom achieves savings by compressing data formats like JSON, eliminating redundant information, and caching compressed payloads to avoid repeated processing. The tool supports both local and enterprise-level deployments, enabling multiple developers to share compressed data and manage token budgets more effectively. This approach addresses common challenges in AI cost management by automating prompt optimization and reducing wasteful token consumption.

items.title: Codacy scans 34,266 repositories and finds 1 in 4 organizations have gaps in AI agent configuration files, including ambiguity, missing failure behavior, and security risks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: 34,266 repos were scanned: 1 in 4 orgs showed gaps in AI agent config files
items.summary:
Codacy analyzed 34,266 repositories across 1,353 organizations to assess how AI agent configuration files are managed. The scan revealed that one in four organizations have significant gaps in these files, including ambiguous instructions, missing failure handling, and security vulnerabilities. These issues pose risks because AI coding assistants rely on these configurations to guide their behavior, and flaws can lead to inconsistent or unsafe code changes.

The study found over 13,000 issues related to clarity, nearly 5,000 related to missing escape hatches for error handling, and about 1,150 security-related problems. Many teams treat agent configuration files as informal documentation rather than enforcing strict standards, which contrasts with the rigor applied to application code. The findings highlight the need for better security controls, clearer instructions, and continuous validation to ensure AI agents operate safely and effectively within software projects.

items.title: Researchers find matrix orthogonalization improves noisy associative recall in recurrent neural networks, enhancing memory performance on synthetic benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Matrix Orthogonalization Improves Memory in Recurrent Models
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that applying matrix orthogonalization to the memory matrices in recurrent neural networks (RNNs), specifically mLSTMs, enhances their performance on noisy associative recall (NAR) tasks. This approach, inspired by techniques used in the Muon optimizer, involves orthogonalizing the memory matrix during read operations without writing back the orthogonalized matrix, leading to improved accuracy and success rates on synthetic benchmarks designed to test memory under noise.

The study compared standard mLSTMs with their orthogonalized variants on next-token prediction tasks using the MAD noisy associative recall suite, which simulates environments with noisy transitions. Results showed that orthogonalization notably improved performance, especially on more challenging tasks with larger vocabularies and longer sequences, suggesting that this method helps prevent weaker memories from being overshadowed during recall.

While these findings are promising, the researchers caution that the improvements were observed in small model regimes and synthetic tasks. Further investigation is needed to determine if these gains translate to larger models and real-world applications. The work highlights a potential pathway to enhance RNN memory capabilities without incurring the computational costs associated with transformer architectures.

items.summary:
The US government has lifted export restrictions on Anthropic's Mythos and Fable AI models, allowing the company to restore public access after weeks of negotiations. Previously, these models were subject to export controls that required special licenses for foreign access, effectively limiting their availability outside the US. The decision follows Anthropic's commitment to collaborate with the government on security protocols and to monitor for malicious use.

The restrictions had been imposed in June, shortly after the models' initial releases, amid concerns about their potential to identify software vulnerabilities. However, the ban was seen by some experts as politically motivated, given Anthropic executives' public criticisms of government AI policies. The easing of restrictions comes as Asian competitors develop similar AI capabilities, prompting US officials to support domestic AI competitiveness.

This development highlights ongoing challenges in US AI policy, as the Trump administration's inconsistent approach has created uncertainty for AI companies regarding future model releases and regulatory oversight. The administration's recent executive order aiming to review AI models before release has also faced criticism from industry analysts.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate AI browsers can be tricked into ignoring safety guardrails by accepting false premises like 2 + 2 = 5, enabling potential data extraction attacks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: New attack provides one more reason why AI browsers are a bad idea
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that AI browsers can be manipulated into ignoring their built-in safety guardrails by accepting false premises, such as the incorrect statement that 2 + 2 = 5. This manipulation lulls the AI into a false reality where it no longer enforces restrictions, potentially allowing attackers to extract sensitive data like private code or credentials. The proof-of-concept exploit involves a malicious website presenting a puzzle that rewards incorrect answers, causing the AI to enter this altered state and bypass its safety measures.

This vulnerability highlights a fundamental issue with current AI browser guardrails, which are reactive and can be circumvented by changing the AI's context rather than addressing underlying risks. The technique, demonstrated on multiple AI browsers, raises concerns about the merging of browsing and AI assistant functions, which could lead to new vectors for data breaches and unauthorized actions. While the current exploit is more a demonstration than a stealthy attack, it underscores the need for more robust security approaches in AI browser design.

items.originalTitle: Agriculture is ready for AI, but its data isn’t
items.summary:
Artificial intelligence holds significant promise for agriculture, offering improvements in crop yield, water use, and chemical application. However, industry experts caution that successful AI adoption depends on establishing a reliable and comprehensive data foundation. Without accurate, consistent, and well-governed data, AI models risk producing misleading recommendations that could harm agricultural operations.

Agriculture presents unique challenges for data integration due to the complexity of modern farming environments, which involve diverse IoT devices, autonomous machinery, and multiple external data sources. Effective AI requires detailed understanding of farm-specific variables such as soil variation and precise field boundaries, as well as robust data governance to ensure information remains current and accurate. Building a unified data model that reflects real-world operations is essential for AI to deliver trustworthy and actionable insights in this sector.

items.originalSummary:
We closely track efforts by Anthropic, Google and OpenAI to get access to more server chips to run their models. But we don’t talk enough about the work these companies are doing to get more juice from the servers they already have.

In one previously unreported example, OpenAI engineers earlier this month told some colleagues they had figured out a way to more than halve the cost of inference, or running existing models, thanks to some newly-discovered optimizations, according to a person with knowledge of those discussions.

When the engineers applied the new techniques to power ChatGPT for visitors who didn’t have a free or paid account, it reduced the number of Nvidia graphics processing units needed at one point to just a couple hundred—a shockingly small number. (That said, OpenAI likely doesn’t get much ChatGPT usage from such users, as the company limits how much they can use the chatbot that way.)

It isn’t clear what OpenAI did to get its latest efficiency gains, which might include techniques such as quantization; key value-caching, or helping the model remember information from prior calculations it made so it doesn’t need to repeat the work; sending queries to be answered in batches rather than one by one; and routing some queries to models or parts of models that require less power to answer them.

The show features real sets and contestants competing in a high-stakes social experiment, with an AI-generated voiceover of Gene Wilder created in collaboration with ElevenLabs and with the consent of Wilder's family.

This production follows Netflix's trend of adapting fictional scenarios into reality competitions, similar to its Squid Game reality show. The series involves 12 contestants and their chosen partners competing for a grand prize, culminating in a two-part finale on September 30th. The project continues Netflix's partnership with the Roald Dahl company and is distinct from the upcoming 2027 animated Charlie and the Chocolate Factory film.

items.title: Google launches Nano Banana 2 Lite, a faster and cheaper AI image generator optimized for high-volume workflows, available via Google AI Studio and Gemini API [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Google introduces a faster, cheaper image generator with Nano Banana 2 Lite
items.summary:
Google has launched Nano Banana 2 Lite, a faster and more affordable version of its AI image generator designed for high-volume workflows. The new model can produce images in about four seconds at a cost of $0.034 per 1,000 images, making it suitable for creators who need to generate and refine large numbers of images quickly. Nano Banana 2 Lite is available through Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, replacing the original Nano Banana model.

This release follows previous versions like Nano Banana 2, which focused on creating more realistic images, and Nano Banana Pro, a more powerful option for advanced use cases. Google positions Nano Banana 2 Lite as optimized for rapid, large-scale image production, supporting creative iteration and multimedia workflows. The company also announced a wider release of Gemini Omni Flash for video generation and introduced Omni Product Studio, an app that converts static images into cinematic e-commerce videos, highlighting Google's continued investment in generative media tools.

items.title: National Design Studio delays Trump’s AI-driven plan to redesign 27,000 government websites after one year, facing criticism over accessibility and limited progress [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Trump's plan to redesign every .gov website leads to AI-designed horrors
items.summary:
The National Design Studio (NDS), established by President Donald Trump to overhaul 27,000 government websites using AI within three years, has faced significant delays and criticism after one year. Despite ambitious goals to modernize the US Web Design System and improve usability, the initiative has made limited progress, with most launched sites being minimal and agencies reluctant to adopt new standards. Experts have raised concerns about the heavy reliance on AI and lack of accessibility compliance testing.

NDS's most notable achievement is updating the federal retirement system, though this project was already underway before the studio's creation. Many newly launched websites consist of single pages or redirect to legacy sites, and some design choices have drawn public scrutiny. The studio's efforts have been hampered by prior cuts to government digital teams and resistance from agencies, casting doubt on the feasibility of the ambitious redesign within the planned timeframe.

items.originalTitle: New KKR Venture Hunts for Deals to Clear Data Center Logjam
items.summary:
Helix Infrastructure Partners, a new AI infrastructure firm backed by KKR, Nvidia, and led by former Amazon Web Services chief Adam Selipsky, is aiming to accelerate the build-out of AI data centers in the U.S. The company plans to acquire existing data center firms that specialize in custom facilities for large cloud customers, leveraging over $10 billion in capital to quickly expand its presence in the market.

Rather than starting from scratch, Helix has already identified a shortlist of potential acquisition targets to address the high demand for data center space among hyperscalers. This move positions Helix among private equity investors actively investing in AI infrastructure to meet the growing needs of cloud and AI service providers.
